{{Short description|Cryptographic attack on the RSA system}}
The '''Wiener's attack''', named after cryptologist Michael J. Wiener, is a type of [[cryptographic attack]] against [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]]. The attack uses [[simple continued fraction|continued fraction representation]] to expose the private key ''d'' when ''d'' is small.

== Background on RSA ==

Fictional characters [[Alice and Bob]] are people who want to communicate securely. More specifically, Alice wants to send a message to Bob which only Bob can read. First Bob chooses two secret [[primes]] ''p'' and ''q''. Then he calculates the RSA [[modular arithmetic|modulus]] {{nowrap|1=''N'' = ''pq''}}. This RSA modulus is made public together with the [[encryption]] exponent ''e''. ''N''  and ''e'' form the public key pair {{nowrap|(''e'', ''N'')}}. By making this information public, anyone can [[encrypt]] messages to Bob. The [[decryption]] exponent ''d'' satisfies {{nowrap|1=''ed'' ≡ 1 (mod ''λ''(''N''))}}, where ''λ''(''N'') denotes the [[Carmichael function]], though sometimes ''φ''(''N''), the [[Euler's totient function]], is used (note: this is the order of the [[multiplicative group]] ('''Z'''{{px2}}/{{px2}}''N'''''Z''')<sup>×</sup>, which is not necessarily a [[cyclic group]]). The encryption exponent ''e'' and ''λ''(''N'') also must be [[coprime|relatively prime]] so that there is a [[Modular multiplicative inverse|modular inverse]]. The [[factorization]] of ''N'' and the private key ''d'' are kept secret, so that only Bob can [[decrypt]] the message. We denote the private key pair as {{nowrap|(''d'', ''N'')}}. The encryption of the message ''M'' is given by {{nowrap|''C'' ≡ ''M''<sup>''e''</sup> (mod ''N'')}} and the decryption of cipher text ''C'' is given by {{nowrap|''C''<sup>''d''</sup> ≡ (''M''<sup>''e''</sup>)<sup>''d''</sup> ≡ ''M''<sup>''ed''</sup> ≡ ''M'' (mod ''N'')}} (using [[Euler's theorem|Euler's Theorem]]).

Using the [[Euclidean algorithm]], one can efficiently recover the secret key ''d'' if one knows the [[factorization]] of ''N''. By having the secret key ''d'', one can efficiently factor the modulus of ''N''.<ref name=LR>[http://personalpages.manchester.ac.uk/postgrad/elaine.render/mathtoday.pdf. L. Render, Elaine (2007). Wiener's Attack on Short Secret Exponents.]{{Dead link|date=April 2022}}</ref>

== Small private key ==

In the RSA [[cryptosystem]], Bob might tend to use a small value of ''d'', rather than a large random number to improve the [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] [[decryption]] performance. However, Wiener's attack shows that choosing a small value for ''d'' will result in an insecure system in which an attacker can recover all secret information, i.e., break the [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] system. This break is based on Wiener's theorem, which holds for small values of ''d''. Wiener has proved that the attacker may efficiently find ''d'' when {{nowrap|''d'' < {{sfrac|1|3}}{{hsp}}''N''<sup>1/4</sup>}}.<ref name=DB/>

Wiener's paper also presented some countermeasures against his attack that allow fast decryption. Two techniques are described as follows.

'''Choosing large public key''':  Replace ''e'' by ''e''′, where {{nowrap|1=''e''′ = ''e'' + ''k'' ⋅ ''λ''(''N'')}} for some large of ''k''. When ''e''′ is large enough, i.e. {{nowrap|''e''′ > ''N''<sup>3/2</sup>}}, then Wiener's attack cannot be applied regardless of how small ''d'' is.

'''Using the [[Chinese remainder theorem]]''':  Suppose one chooses ''d'' such that both {{nowrap|''d''<sub>''p''</sub> ≡ ''d'' (mod (''p'' − 1))}} and {{nowrap|''d''<sub>''q''</sub> ≡ ''d'' (mod (''q'' − 1))}} are small but ''d'' itself is not, then a fast [[decryption]] of ''C'' can be done as follows:
# First compute {{nowrap|''M''<sub>''p''</sub> ≡ ''C''<sup>''d''<sub>''p''</sub></sup> (mod ''p'')}} and {{nowrap|''M''<sub>''q''</sub> ≡ ''C''<sup>''d''<sub>''q''</sub></sup> (mod ''q'')}}.
# Use the  [[Chinese remainder theorem]] to compute the unique value of {{nowrap|0 ≤ ''M'' < ''N''}} that satisfies {{nowrap|''M'' ≡ ''M''<sub>''p''</sub> (mod ''p'')}} and {{nowrap|''M'' ≡ ''M''<sub>''q''</sub> (mod ''q''}}. The result of ''M'' satisfies {{nowrap|''M'' ≡ ''C''<sup>''d''</sup> (mod ''N'')}} as needed. The point is that Wiener's attack does not apply here because the value of {{nowrap|''d'' mod ''λ''(''N'')}} can be large.{{cn|date=October 2024}}

{{See also|RSA (algorithm)#Using the Chinese remainder algorithm}}

== How the attack works ==

Note that
: <math> \lambda(N) = \operatorname{lcm}(p-1, q-1) = \frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{G} = \frac{\varphi(N)}{G}</math>
where {{nowrap|1=''G'' = gcd(''p'' − 1, ''q'' − 1)}}. 

Since {{nowrap|''ed'' ≡ 1 (mod ''λ''(''N''))}}, there exists an integer ''K'' such that
: <math> ed = K \times \lambda(N)+1 </math>
: <math> ed = \frac {K}{G} (p-1)(q-1)+1 </math>

Defining {{nowrap|1=''k'' = {{sfrac|''K''|gcd(''K'', ''G'')}}}} and {{nowrap|1=''g'' = {{sfrac|''G''|gcd(''K'', ''G'')}}}}, and substituting into the above gives:
: <math>ed = \frac {k}{g} (p-1) (q-1)+1</math>.
Divided by ''dpq'':
: <math>\frac{e}{pq} = \frac{k}{dg} (1- \delta)</math>, where <math>\delta = \frac {p+q-1- \frac {g}{k}}{pq} </math>.

So, {{sfrac|''e''|''pq''}} is slightly smaller than {{sfrac|''k''|''dg''}}, and the former is composed entirely of public [[information]]. However, a method of checking{{Clarify|date=April 2022}} and guess is still required.

By using simple [[algebra]]ic manipulations and [[identity (mathematics)|identities]], a guess can be checked for [[accuracy]].<ref name=LR/>

== Wiener's theorem ==
Let {{nowrap|1=''N'' = ''pq''}} with {{nowrap|''q'' < ''p'' < 2''q''}}. Let {{nowrap|''d'' < {{sfrac|1|3}}{{hsp}}''N''<sup>1/4</sup>}}.

Given {{nowrap|{{angbr|''N'', ''e''}}}} with {{nowrap|''ed'' ≡ 1 (mod ''λ''(''N''))}}, the attacker can efficiently recover ''d''.<ref name=DB>{{cite journal
|author-last=Boneh
|author-first=Dan
|author-link=Dan Boneh
|title=Twenty years of attacks on the RSA cryptosystem
|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199902/boneh.pdf
|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]
|volume=46
|issue=2
|pages=203–213
}}</ref><ref name="Wiener1999">{{cite journal
|last1=Wiener
|first1=Michael J.
|date=1990
|title=Cryptanalysis of short RSA secret exponents
|journal= IEEE Transactions on Information Theory
|volume=36
|issue=3
|pages=553–558
|doi=10.1109/18.54902
|publisher=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|IEEE]]
|bibcode=1990ITIT...36..553W
}}</ref>

== Example ==
{{confusing|section|reason=it assumes ''ed'' ≡ 1 (mod ''φ''(''N'')), unlike the rest of the article, which uses (mod ''λ''(''N'')) instead|date=April 2022}}
Suppose that the public keys are {{nowrap|1={{angbr|''N'', ''e''}} = {{angbr|90581, 17993}}}}. The attack should determine ''d''. By using Wiener's theorem and [[continued fractions]] to approximate ''d'', first we try to find the [[continued fractions]] expansion of {{sfrac|''e''|''N''}}. Note that this algorithm finds [[fractions]] in their lowest terms. We know that
: <math>\frac{e}{N} = \frac{17993}{90581} = \cfrac{1}{5 + \cfrac{1}{29 +\dots + \cfrac{1}{3}}} = \left [0,5,29,4,1,3,2,4,3 \right ]</math>

According to the [[continued fraction]]s expansion of {{sfrac|''e''|''N''}}, all convergents {{sfrac|''k''|''d''}} are:
: <math> \frac{k}{d} = 0, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{29}{146}, \frac{117}{589}, \frac{146}{735}, \frac{555}{2794}, \frac{1256}{6323}, \frac{5579}{28086}, \frac{17993}{90581}</math>

We can verify that the first [[convergent (continued fraction)|convergent]] does not produce a factorization of ''N''. However, the convergent {{sfrac|1|5}} yields
: <math> \varphi (N) = \frac{ed - 1}{k} = \frac{17993\times5 - 1}{1} = 89964</math>
Now, if we solve the equation
: <math>x^2 - \left ( \left (N - \varphi (N) \right ) + 1 \right )x + N = 0</math>
: <math>x^2 - \left ( \left (90581 - 89964 \right ) + 1 \right )x + 90581 = 0</math>
: <math>x^2 - 618x + 90581 = 0</math>
then we find the [[Equation solving|roots]] which are {{nowrap|1=''x'' = 379; 239}}. Therefore we have found the factorization
: <math>N = 90581 = 379 \times 239 = p \times q</math>.
Notice that, for the modulus {{nowrap|1=''N'' = 90581}}, Wiener's theorem will work if
: <math>d < \frac{N^{1/4}}{3} \approx 5.7828</math>.

== Proof of Wiener's theorem ==
The proof is based on approximations using continued fractions.<ref name=DB />

Since {{nowrap|1=''ed'' = 1 (mod ''λ''(''N''))}}, there exists a ''k'' such that {{nowrap|1=''ed'' − ''kλ''(''N'') = 1}}. Therefore
: <math>\left | \frac {e}{\lambda (N)}- \frac {k}{d}  \right \vert = \frac{1}{d \lambda (N)}</math>.

Let {{nowrap|1=''G'' = gcd(''p'' − 1, ''q'' − 1)}}; note that if ''φ''(''N'') is used instead of ''λ''(''N''), then the proof can be replaced with {{nowrap|1=''G'' = 1}} and ''φ''(''N'') replaced with ''λ''(''N'').

Then multiplying by {{sfrac|1|''G''}},
: <math>\left | \frac {e}{\varphi (N)}- \frac {k}{Gd}  \right \vert = \frac{1}{d \varphi (N)}</math>

Hence, {{sfrac|''k''|''Gd''}} is an approximation of {{sfrac|''e''|''φ''(''N'')}}. Although the attacker does not know ''φ''(''N''), he may use ''N'' to approximate it. Indeed, since {{nowrap|1=''φ''(''N'') = ''N'' − ''p'' − ''q'' + 1}} and {{nowrap|''p'' + ''q'' − 1 < 3{{sqrt|''N''}}}}, we have:
: <math>\left \vert p+q-1 \right \vert < 3 \sqrt{N}</math>
: <math>\left \vert N-\varphi (N) \right \vert < 3 \sqrt{N}</math>

Using ''N'' in place of ''φ''(''N'') we obtain:
: <math>\begin{align}
\left \vert \frac{e}{N}- \frac{k}{Gd} \right \vert &= \left \vert \frac{edG-kN}{NGd} \right \vert \\
&= \left \vert \frac{edG-k \varphi (N)-kN+k \varphi (N)}{NGd} \right \vert \\
&= \left \vert \frac{1-k(N- \varphi (N))}{NGd} \right \vert \\
&< \left \vert \frac{-k(N- \varphi (N))}{NGd} \right \vert (\because 0 < |N-\varphi (N)|)\\
&< \left \vert \frac{3k \sqrt{N}}{NGd} \right \vert = \frac {3k \sqrt{N}}{\sqrt{N} \sqrt{N}Gd} \le \frac {3k}{d \sqrt{N}}
\end{align}
</math>

Now, {{nowrap|1=''kλ''(''N'') = ''ed'' − 1 < ''ed''}}, so {{nowrap|''kλ''(''N'') < ''ed''}}. Since {{nowrap|''e'' < ''λ''(''N'')}}, so {{nowrap|''kλ''(''N'') < ''ed'' < ''λ''(''N'')''d''}}, then we obtain:  
: <math>k \lambda (N)<\lambda (N)d</math>
::: <math>k<d</math>

Since {{nowrap|''k'' < ''d''}} and {{nowrap|''d'' < {{sfrac|1|3}}{{hsp}}''N''<sup>1/4</sup>}}.
Hence we obtain:
: (1) <math>\left \vert \frac{e}{N}- \frac{k}{Gd} \right \vert < \frac{1}{dN^{\frac{1}{4}}}</math>

Since {{nowrap|''d'' < {{sfrac|1|3}}{{hsp}}''N''<sup>1/4</sup>}}, {{nowrap|2''d'' < 3''d''}}, then {{nowrap|2''d'' < 3''d'' < ''N''<sup>1/4</sup>}}, we obtain:
: <math>2d<N^{1/4}</math>, so (2) <math>\frac{1}{2d} > \frac{1}{N^{1/4}}</math>
From (1) and (2), we can conclude that
: <math>\left \vert \frac{e}{N}- \frac{k}{Gd} \right \vert < \frac{3k}{d \sqrt{N}}< \frac{1}{d \cdot 2d}= \frac{1}{2d^2}</math>

If {{nowrap|{{abs|''x'' − {{sfrac|''a''|''b''}}}} < {{sfrac|1|2''b''<sup>2</sup>}}}}, then {{sfrac|''a''|''b''}} is a convergent of ''x'', thus {{sfrac|''k''|''Gd''}} appears among the convergents of {{sfrac|''e''|''N''}}. Therefore the algorithm will indeed eventually find {{sfrac|''k''|''Gd''}}.

{{Explain|reason=How do you obtain (k, d) from k/Gd? The cited sources only consider the easy case of G = 1.|date=April 2022}}
